questions.title: How do localStorage and sessionStorage work, and what are their limits?
questions.description: localStorage and sessionStorage are both part of the Storage API, and they let you save small pieces of text data directly in the browser, without needing a server. They work almost the same way: you use setItem(key, value) to save a value, getItem(key) to read it back, and removeItem(key) to delete it. The difference is how long the data stays. localStorage keeps the data even after you close the browser and open it again later. sessionStorage only keeps the data for as long as that one browser tab stays open: it survives a page reload, but every tab gets its own separate sessionStorage, and it is cleared when the tab is closed. Data in both is stored per origin (protocol + domain + port), so one website cannot read another website's storage. Both can only store strings, so if you want to save an object or an array, you need to convert it to a string first (usually with JSON.stringify), and convert it back when you read it (with JSON.parse). They also have a storage limit, usually around 5 megabytes per website, depending on the browser. Both are synchronous (reading and writing block other code for a moment) and readable by any script on the page, so they should never hold sensitive data like passwords or tokens.
keyPoints: setItem(key, value), getItem(key), and removeItem(key) are the main methods for both.
localStorage keeps data even after the browser is closed and reopened.
sessionStorage only keeps data for as long as the current tab stays open (it survives a reload, and each tab has its own).
Both only store strings, so objects/arrays need JSON.stringify() to save and JSON.parse() to read back.
Storage is limited, usually a few megabytes per website.

questions.title: What are cookies, and how do you work with them in JavaScript?
questions.description: A cookie is a small piece of text data that a website can store in the browser, similar to localStorage, but with one big difference: cookies are also automatically sent to the server with every HTTP request to that website. This makes cookies useful for things like keeping a user logged in, or remembering a setting, because the server can read the cookie on every request without JavaScript having to do anything extra. You can read and write cookies from JavaScript using document.cookie, but the format is a bit awkward. Reading it gives you all cookies together in one single string, separated by semicolons, so you usually need a small helper function to get just one cookie. Writing to it, like document.cookie = "theme=dark", adds or updates only that one cookie, without removing the others. Values with special characters should be encoded with encodeURIComponent. Each cookie is limited to about 4 KB. Cookies can also have an expiration date (expires or max-age; without one, the cookie is deleted when the browser closes), and extra safety flags like secure (only sent over HTTPS), SameSite (limits sending the cookie with requests coming from other websites), or httpOnly (cannot be read from JavaScript at all, only sent by the browser automatically — this flag can only be set by the server).
keyPoints: A cookie is a small piece of text, similar to localStorage, but it is also sent to the server with every request automatically.
Cookies are common for things like login sessions and remembering user settings.
Reading document.cookie gives all cookies as one combined string, separated by semicolons; writing to it adds or updates a single cookie.
Cookies can have an expiration date, and extra safety flags like secure, SameSite, or httpOnly (set only by the server).
